programs.name: EDI, SB 35, and AB 2011 Streamlined Affordable Financing
programs.description: Ministerial approval pathways for 100% affordable and qualifying mixed-income projects. LA Executive Directive 1 (ED1) is the city-specific layer; SB 35 and AB 2011 are statewide pathways that apply in every California jurisdiction.
typical_stack: Construction loan (bank, CDFI, or mission-focused lender)
4% or 9% LIHTC equity
Tax-exempt bond financing (for 4% deals)
State soft debt: HHAP, NPLH, AHSC, or MHP depending on project profile
City / county soft debt (trust funds, linkage fees, HOME, CDBG)
Sponsor equity and deferred developer fee

key_features.ceqa_treatment: Exempt or streamlined for qualifying projects
key_features.parking_requirements: Reduced or waived in most cases
key_features.prevailing_wage: Required for most paths (SB 35, AB 2011, all LIHTC)
key_features.affordability_covenant: 55 years (LIHTC baseline) or longer depending on program

programs.name: 4% LIHTC and Tax-Exempt Bond Financing
programs.description: The non-competitive 4% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, available with tax-exempt private activity bond financing. Fixed 4% floor since the 2021 federal legislation made the credit mathematically favorable for larger affordable developments.
typical_stack: Construction loan (often the same lender as bond issuer on single-close structures)
Tax-exempt private activity bond issuance (bond-financed deal qualifies for 4% credit)
4% LIHTC investor equity (~30% of TDC)
State soft debt: MHP, AHSC, NPLH where applicable
Local soft debt: city trust funds, linkage fees, HOME
Sponsor equity and deferred developer fee

key_features.allocation: Non-competitive, automatic with qualifying bond financing
key_features.scoring: No competitive scoring round; CDLAC bond allocation is gating
key_features.minimum_deal_size: Practical floor around $15M TDC due to bond issuance overhead

programs.name: 9% Competitive LIHTC Financing
programs.description: The competitive 9% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, allocated through the state housing finance agency via scoring rounds. Delivers roughly 70% of development cost as equity, but requires a winning scoring profile in an increasingly competitive field.
typical_stack: Construction loan (bank, CDFI, or mission-focused lender)
9% LIHTC investor equity (~70% of TDC)
Permanent loan (smaller than 4% deals because credit equity is larger)
State soft debt: MHP, AHSC, HHAP, NPLH for qualifying profiles
Local soft debt where needed to close the gap
Sponsor equity and deferred developer fee

key_features.allocation: Competitive scoring through state HFA rounds
key_features.scoring_dynamics: Multiple rounds per year; winning threshold varies by set-aside and region
key_features.tcac_region_matters: Region-specific scoring and set-asides create different competitive dynamics
key_features.timing_risk: Multiple application rounds may be needed before allocation

programs.name: Tax-Exempt Bond Financing for Affordable Multifamily
programs.description: Private activity bonds issued by qualifying local, state, or regional bond issuers to finance affordable multifamily. Bond financing automatically qualifies the project for 4% LIHTC and can serve as both construction and permanent financing.
typical_stack: Tax-exempt bond issuance (construction phase)
4% LIHTC investor equity
Permanent bond issuance or conversion to permanent debt at stabilization
State soft debt layering
Local soft debt layering
Sponsor equity and deferred developer fee

key_features.issuer_types: Local agencies, regional authorities, state housing finance agencies
key_features.allocation: State housing finance agency allocates private activity bond cap annually
key_features.bond_structure: Often issued as variable-rate demand obligations or fixed-rate bonds, with credit enhancement from letter of credit or bond insurance
key_features.lihtc_coupling: Bond-financed deals automatically qualify for 4% LIHTC
key_features.minimum_deal_size: Practical floor around $15M TDC due to issuance costs
key_features.affordability_covenant: 55 years, often longer depending on issuer

programs.name: Transit-Oriented Communities (TOC) and Density Bonus Affordable Financing
programs.description: Los Angeles Transit-Oriented Communities program and the California Density Bonus Law provide entitlement bonuses for affordable housing projects near high-quality transit. TOC Tiers 1 through 4 (based on transit proximity) deliver density bonuses of 22.5% to 70%+ above base zoning, reduced parking, and ministerial approval when layered with Executive Directive 1 or SB 35. Most TOC projects layer LIHTC, city soft debt, and state gap financing against the additional density to close the capital gap.
typical_stack: TOC or Density Bonus entitlement (by-right or ministerial for qualifying projects)
Construction loan (bank, CDFI, or tax-exempt bond issuer)
4% or 9% LIHTC investor equity depending on deal size and competitive profile
AHSC (Affordable Housing and Sustainable Communities) soft debt: transit-adjacent projects score well
City soft debt: LA Affordable Housing Trust Fund, Linkage Fee, HOME, CDBG
Sponsor equity and deferred developer fee

key_features.density_bonus_tiers: TOC Tier 1: 22.5% above base FAR; Tier 2: 32.5%; Tier 3: 45%; Tier 4: 70%+
key_features.transit_proximity: Tier 1: 1/4 mile from local bus; up to Tier 4: 1/4 mile from high-quality rail
key_features.affordable_set_aside: Typically 11-25% of base units at 30-80% AMI depending on tier and bonuses requested
key_features.parking_reduction: Significant reduction or elimination for units within 1/2 mile of transit
key_features.ceqa_treatment: Categorically exempt or streamlined for qualifying projects
key_features.california_density_bonus_law: State DBL (Government Code 65915) applies statewide; TOC is the LA-specific overlay

programs.name: HUD 221(d)(4) Multifamily Construction-to-Permanent Financing
programs.description: HUD Section 221(d)(4) provides FHA-insured, non-recourse construction-to-permanent mortgage financing for multifamily projects of five or more units. The program offers up to 87.5% LTC for market-rate and 90% LTC for affordable projects, with a 40-year fully amortizing term at a fixed rate. It is the most favorable long-term capital available for affordable and workforce multifamily construction when the timeline and complexity can be absorbed.
typical_stack: HUD 221(d)(4) first mortgage (FHA-insured, non-recourse, construction-to-perm)
4% or 9% LIHTC investor equity where affordable set-asides qualify
Tax-exempt bond financing (often the same lender as HUD MAP lender on single-close structures)
State soft debt: MHP, AHSC, NPLH where eligible
Local soft debt: city housing trust funds, HOME, CDBG
Sponsor equity and deferred developer fee

key_features.ltc: Up to 87.5% for market-rate; 90% for affordable (50%+ affordable units at 80% AMI or below)
key_features.term: 40 years fully amortizing plus construction period (typically 24-36 months)
key_features.rate: Fixed rate set at loan commitment; long-term favorable rate
key_features.recourse: Non-recourse except for standard carve-outs (fraud, waste, environmental)
key_features.davis_bacon: Federal prevailing wage (Davis-Bacon) required on all HUD-insured construction projects
key_features.timeline: Typically 12-18 months from application to construction closing; not suited for time-sensitive deals
key_features.map_lender: Must use an FHA-approved MAP (Multifamily Accelerated Processing) lender

programs.name: Permanent Supportive Housing (PSH) Financing
programs.description: Permanent supportive housing provides housing with integrated supportive services for people experiencing homelessness, those with chronic homelessness, or individuals with serious mental illness or substance use disorders. PSH financing layers capital from Proposition HHH (Los Angeles), NPLH (No Place Like Home), HHAP (Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention), LIHTC, and Section 8 project-based vouchers. These deals are among the most complex capital stacks in affordable housing, typically involving six or more funding sources.
typical_stack: Construction loan (CDFI, community development bank, or HUD 221(d)(4) for larger deals)
NPLH (No Place Like Home) capital: $30,000 to $60,000 per unit for qualified permanent supportive housing
HHAP: Local homeless housing assistance and prevention funds from city or county
Proposition HHH (Los Angeles only): City bond proceeds for permanent supportive housing
9% LIHTC equity (strong PSH projects score well in most state HFA rounds)
Section 8 project-based vouchers (HUD VASH or CoC-sponsored) as permanent operating subsidy
Sponsor equity and deferred developer fee

key_features.target_population: Chronically homeless, seriously mentally ill, veterans (HUD-VASH), transition-age youth
key_features.nplh_funding: $2B California statewide; $30,000 to $60,000 per unit for qualifying PSH projects
key_features.prop_hhh: LA-specific: $1.2B bond measure for PSH; LAHD administers; winding down as of 2026
key_features.section_8_pbv: Project-based vouchers are the permanent operating subsidy; CoC or PHA-administered
key_features.services_requirement: Operator must demonstrate supportive services capacity; LAHSA or county approval often required
key_features.tcac_scoring: PSH projects score well in 9% LIHTC competitive rounds due to homeless set-aside and special needs points

programs.name: Workforce Housing and NOAH Preservation Financing
programs.description: Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing (NOAH) preservation and workforce housing financing covers acquisition and rehabilitation of older multifamily properties serving households earning 60-120% of Area Median Income without relying on government subsidy. These deals use conventional debt, bridge loans, agency financing, mezzanine capital, and in some cases 4% LIHTC with regulatory agreement to protect affordability. Workforce housing is the largest segment of the affordable housing universe by unit count.
programs.typical_deal_range: $5M to $75M acquisition or total development cost
typical_stack: Acquisition or rehab bridge loan (bank, CDFI, or private lender)
Permanent agency debt (Freddie Mac TEL, Fannie Mae MTEB, or conventional permanent mortgage)
4% LIHTC investor equity (where income restrictions are accepted in exchange for below-market equity)
Mezzanine debt or preferred equity for gap coverage
State soft debt where workforce income limits qualify
Local inclusionary fund or housing trust proceeds where available

key_features.ami_range: Serves households at 60-120% AMI; bridge between deep subsidy and market-rate
key_features.lihtc_option: 4% LIHTC available where developer accepts 55-year rent restrictions at 60% AMI for qualifying units
key_features.noah_preservation: Preserves older multifamily (1960-1990 vintage) at risk of conversion to market-rate or luxury rehab
key_features.freddie_tl: Freddie Mac Targeted Affordable Housing (TAH) and Tax-Exempt Loan (TEL) programs support NOAH deals
key_features.no_subsidy_required: Deals can close without government subsidy; faster timeline than LIHTC transactions
key_features.regulatory_agreement: Optional affordability covenant traded for soft debt access; typically 10-30 year term

seo.title_suffix: Workforce Housing and NOAH Preservation Financing
seo.meta_template: How workforce housing and NOAH preservation financing works in {city}. Bridge loans, agency debt, 4% LIHTC options, and the lenders who close these deals.

programs.name: Opportunity Zone and Affordable LIHTC Overlay Financing
programs.description: Opportunity Zone (OZ) equity can be layered with Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) financing when a project is located in a designated Qualified Opportunity Zone and meets both LIHTC affordable use requirements and the OZ substantial improvement test. These combined structures allow sponsors to access two federal tax incentive programs simultaneously, typically reducing the required permanent debt load and improving deal economics for patient equity investors.
typical_stack: Opportunity Zone equity (Qualified Opportunity Fund investment in the operating or property entity)
4% or 9% LIHTC investor equity
Tax-exempt bond financing (for 4% LIHTC deals)
Construction loan (bank or CDFI, often from the same lender as bond issuer)
State and local soft debt where OZ location and LIHTC restrictions are compatible
Permanent first mortgage or bond conversion at stabilization

key_features.oz_benefit: OZ investors defer capital gains taxes until 2026 and exclude post-investment gains after 10-year hold
key_features.lihtc_overlay: LIHTC investor equity reduces the OZ equity requirement, improving economics for both capital sources
key_features.10_year_hold: OZ requires 10-year hold of investment, which aligns naturally with the LIHTC compliance period
key_features.qualified_opportunity_zone: Project must be in a designated QOZ tract; 2018 IRS census tract designations apply
key_features.complexity: Dual-compliance (LIHTC and OZ) requires specialized legal and tax counsel; limited lender pool active in this niche
key_features.competitiveness: Fewer sponsors pursue OZ plus LIHTC; capital is less competitive than standalone LIHTC for patient equity investors

seo.title_suffix: Opportunity Zone and Affordable LIHTC Overlay Financing

cities.name: Los Angeles
cities.jurisdictional_notes: City of Los Angeles has the most aggressive ministerial approval regime in California via Executive Directive 1. LA Housing Department (LAHD) administers the Affordable Housing Trust Fund, Linkage Fee revenue, Measure H and HHH proceeds. LA County administers HHAP-LA. Inclusionary Zoning is effectively through the Transit-Oriented Communities program and density bonus overlays.
cities.active_programs_local: Executive Directive 1 (ED1), Transit-Oriented Communities (TOC), SB 8 replacement housing requirements, LA Housing Trust Fund, Linkage Fee, Proposition HHH (permanent supportive housing, winding down)
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Koreatown, Boyle Heights, South LA, San Fernando Valley (Van Nuys, Panorama City, Pacoima), Westlake, Mid-City, Inglewood-adjacent

cities.name: San Francisco
cities.jurisdictional_notes: City and County of San Francisco has the Mayor's Office of Housing and Community Development (MOHCD) administering Jobs-Housing Linkage Program (JHLP), Inclusionary Housing Fund, and other local sources. The city's Density Bonus and Affordable Housing Bonus Program provide entitlement pathways. SB 35 approvals have been increasingly utilized.
cities.active_programs_local: Inclusionary Housing Program, Jobs-Housing Linkage Program, MOHCD Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA), Educator Housing Fund, Housing Accelerator Fund
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Mission, Bayview-Hunters Point, SoMa, Tenderloin, Outer Mission, Visitacion Valley, Treasure Island

cities.name: Oakland
cities.jurisdictional_notes: City of Oakland Department of Housing and Community Development administers Affordable Housing Trust Fund, inclusionary housing program, and Measure KK / U / W bond proceeds. Alameda County administers regional HHAP distribution. Oakland has been one of the most active adopters of SB 35 and AB 2011.
cities.active_programs_local: Affordable Housing Trust Fund, Measure KK / U / W bond proceeds, inclusionary zoning in-lieu fee, Oakland Housing Authority project-based vouchers
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Fruitvale, East Oakland, West Oakland, North Oakland, San Antonio, Eastlake

cities.name: San Diego
cities.jurisdictional_notes: San Diego Housing Commission administers Affordable Housing Fund, rental assistance, and local gap financing. City of San Diego inclusionary housing ordinance, Complete Communities program providing density and incentive bonuses. San Diego County administers HHAP-SD. CDLAC bond allocation through CMFA or local issuers.
cities.active_programs_local: Affordable Housing Fund, Complete Communities Housing Solutions, inclusionary housing, San Diego Housing Commission project-based vouchers, regional HHAP
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Barrio Logan, City Heights, Southeast San Diego, Linda Vista, Mid-City, Escondido, Chula Vista, National City

cities.name: San Jose
cities.jurisdictional_notes: San Jose Housing Department administers Affordable Housing Investment Plan, Measure E real property transfer tax proceeds, and inclusionary housing. Santa Clara County Measure A housing bond proceeds distributed to qualifying projects. SB 35 has been heavily utilized in San Jose.
cities.active_programs_local: Measure E transfer tax proceeds, Measure A county housing bond, Affordable Housing Investment Plan, inclusionary housing program, Notice of Funding Availability cycles
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: East San Jose, Alum Rock, Downtown San Jose, Berryessa, Japantown-adjacent, West San Jose near VTA corridors

cities.name: Sacramento
cities.jurisdictional_notes: Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency (SHRA) administers Affordable Housing Fund, HOME, CDBG, and project-based voucher programs for both City and County. Sacramento County administers HHAP-SAC. Sacramento is a priority market for state HCD due to Central Valley housing needs and capital city status.
cities.active_programs_local: SHRA Affordable Housing Fund, SHRA Multifamily Lending Program, inclusionary housing, Sacramento Housing Authority project-based vouchers, regional HHAP
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Oak Park, Del Paso Heights, Meadowview, North Sacramento, Florin, Arden-Arcade, South Sacramento, Downtown / Midtown infill

cities.name: Long Beach
cities.jurisdictional_notes: Long Beach Housing Authority administers the locally managed Housing Choice Voucher program and project-based vouchers. Long Beach Development Services administers inclusionary zoning, density bonus applications, and local funding programs. Long Beach is one of the most active affordable housing development markets in Southern California outside the City of LA, with strong LIHTC deal flow and active CDLAC bond allocation.
cities.active_programs_local: Long Beach Affordable Housing Trust Fund, inclusionary housing in-lieu fees, Long Beach Housing Authority project-based vouchers, HOME and CDBG entitlement, regional HHAP-LA distribution
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Central Long Beach, North Long Beach, West Long Beach, Downtown Long Beach (transit-proximate sites near Blue Line), Wrigley, Willmore

cities.name: Riverside
cities.jurisdictional_notes: City of Riverside Community and Economic Development Department administers local affordable housing programs. Riverside County Economic Development Agency oversees regional affordable housing funding. The Inland Empire TCAC region is less competitive than coastal regions, which can improve 9% LIHTC scoring odds for qualifying projects. Riverside has seen significant affordable development activity driven by lower land costs and strong state HCD prioritization of inland valley housing production.
cities.active_programs_local: Riverside Affordable Housing Trust Fund, HOME and CDBG entitlement programs, Riverside County EDA affordable housing programs, regional HHAP-IE
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Downtown Riverside, Casa Blanca, Eastside, University corridor, Arlington, Jurupa Valley adjacent

cities.name: Fresno
cities.jurisdictional_notes: City of Fresno Department of Public Works and Planning administers affordable housing entitlements. Fresno Housing Authority is one of the most active PHAs in the state for affordable development, administering both the Housing Choice Voucher program and project-based voucher allocations. The Central Valley TCAC region is a priority for state HCD and typically offers favorable scoring dynamics for 9% LIHTC applications targeting farmworker, extremely low income, and rural populations.
cities.active_programs_local: Fresno Housing Authority project-based vouchers, HOME and CDBG entitlement, Central Valley HHAP allocation, state HCD infill infrastructure grants, Fresno County Housing Programs
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Downtown Fresno, West Fresno, Tower District, Chinatown-adjacent, Calwa, Lowell, Highway City

cities.name: Anaheim
cities.jurisdictional_notes: City of Anaheim Planning and Building Department administers affordable housing approvals. Anaheim Housing Authority administers local voucher programs and project-based vouchers. Orange County is one of the most expensive rental markets in the US, creating strong affordable housing need. TCAC Region 7 includes all of Orange County and competes for a distinct regional allocation, which historically has lower overall competition than Los Angeles County.
cities.active_programs_local: Anaheim Affordable Housing Trust Fund, inclusionary housing program, Anaheim Housing Authority project-based vouchers, Orange County Housing Trust, OC HHAP regional distribution
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Anaheim Resort District-adjacent, West Anaheim, Central Anaheim, Platinum Triangle (transit-proximate near ARTIC), East Anaheim

cities.name: Pasadena
cities.jurisdictional_notes: City of Pasadena Housing Department administers local affordable housing programs, inclusionary zoning, and density bonus applications. Pasadena is a charter city with its own planning authority and has been an active user of SB 35 ministerial approval. The city's Affordable Housing Agreement program requires inclusionary units or in-lieu fee payments. The Metro Gold Line (A Line) provides significant TOC and transit-oriented development opportunities.
cities.active_programs_local: Pasadena Affordable Housing Trust Fund, inclusionary zoning or in-lieu fee, Pasadena Community Development Commission programs, Metro A Line TOC opportunities, HOME and CDBG entitlement
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Old Pasadena-adjacent, Northwest Pasadena, Northwest Rosemead Blvd corridor, Fair Oaks corridor, Sierra Madre Villa station area

cities.name: Stockton
cities.jurisdictional_notes: City of Stockton Community Development Department administers affordable housing entitlements. Stockton Housing Authority administers Section 8 and project-based vouchers. San Joaquin County oversees regional HOME and CDBG distribution. Stockton is a priority city for state HCD due to high poverty rates, historical disinvestment, and low overall housing production. 9% LIHTC applications targeting ELI households score well in the Central Valley region.
cities.active_programs_local: Stockton Affordable Housing Trust Fund, San Joaquin County HOME program, Stockton Housing Authority project-based vouchers, state HCD infill infrastructure, regional HHAP-Central Valley
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Downtown Stockton, South Stockton, Victory Park, Lincoln Village, Weston Ranch, Morada

cities.name: San Bernardino
cities.jurisdictional_notes: City of San Bernardino Planning Division administers affordable housing entitlements. The city emerged from bankruptcy in 2012 and has significant HUD entitlement funding through HOME and CDBG. San Bernardino County has an active Housing and Community Development division. The Inland Empire TCAC region offers competitive scoring opportunities for projects targeting rural, farmworker, and extremely low-income populations.
cities.active_programs_local: San Bernardino HOME and CDBG entitlement, San Bernardino County Housing and Community Development, Housing Authority of the County of San Bernardino (HACSB) project-based vouchers, Inland Empire HHAP
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Downtown San Bernardino, Westside, Inland Center-adjacent, Waterman, Highland-adjacent, Loma Linda adjacent

cities.name: Bakersfield
cities.jurisdictional_notes: City of Bakersfield Planning Division administers affordable housing entitlements. Kern County Housing Authority is the primary PHA for project-based vouchers and Section 8 administration. Bakersfield is a high-growth city with significant affordable housing need driven by agricultural worker households and rapid population growth. The Central Valley TCAC region prioritizes farmworker, agricultural, and ELI applications with dedicated set-asides.
cities.active_programs_local: Kern County Housing Authority project-based vouchers, HOME and CDBG through Kern County, state HCD infill infrastructure grants, HHAP-Central Valley, farmworker housing set-asides through TCAC
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Downtown Bakersfield, East Bakersfield, Oildale-adjacent, Southeast Bakersfield, Rosedale, Greenfield

cities.name: Philadelphia
cities.jurisdictional_notes: Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation (PHDC) and the Division of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) administer local soft debt, HOME, CDBG, and gap financing programs. The Philadelphia Housing Authority (PHA) is one of the largest PHAs in the nation with an active project-based voucher program. PHFA administers 4% and 9% LIHTC statewide, with Philadelphia designated as a Difficult Development Area, and manages the Keystone HOME program and other Pennsylvania-specific soft debt sources.
cities.active_programs_local: Philadelphia Housing Trust Fund, DHCD gap financing, PHA project-based vouchers, HOME and CDBG entitlement, Neighborhood Preservation Initiative, Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority land disposition, Affordable Housing Master Fund
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: North Philadelphia, Kensington, West Philadelphia, Germantown, Frankford, South Philadelphia, Point Breeze, Strawberry Mansion, Grays Ferry

cities.name: New York City
cities.state_hfa: New York State Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) / NYC Housing Development Corporation (HDC) / NYC Department of HPD
cities.jurisdictional_notes: New York City has its own affordable housing finance infrastructure operating alongside the state HFA. HPD (Department of Housing Preservation and Development) administers local soft debt, the City's affordable housing loan programs, and project approvals. HDC (Housing Development Corporation) is the city's bond issuer and lender for tax-exempt bond deals. HCR administers statewide LIHTC allocations. NYC's Extremely Low and Low Income Affordability (ELLA) and Mixed-Income Market Terms (MIMT) programs provide gap financing. NYC is the largest affordable housing market in the US with unique programs not available elsewhere.
cities.active_programs_local: HPD Extremely Low and Low Income Affordability (ELLA), HPD Mixed-Income Market Terms (MIMT), HDC tax-exempt bond issuance, NYC Housing Trust Fund, NYC Affordable Housing Preservation Fund, Inclusionary Housing Program, mandatory inclusionary housing in certain rezoning areas
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: South Bronx, East Harlem, Central Harlem, Brownsville (Brooklyn), East New York, Far Rockaway (Queens), Staten Island North Shore, Washington Heights, Jamaica (Queens)

cities.name: Chicago
cities.jurisdictional_notes: Chicago Department of Housing (DOH) administers local affordable housing programs, the Affordable Requirements Ordinance (ARO), Tax Increment Financing (TIF) for affordable projects, and the Chicago Community Land Trust. The Chicago Housing Authority (CHA) administers project-based vouchers and is one of the most active PHAs for affordable development partnerships. IHDA administers 4% and 9% LIHTC for Illinois, with Chicago receiving the largest share of statewide allocations. Illinois also has dedicated bond cap through the Illinois Finance Authority.
cities.active_programs_local: Chicago Department of Housing gap financing, Affordable Requirements Ordinance (ARO) in-lieu fees and on-site units, CHA project-based vouchers, TIF affordable housing set-asides, Chicago Low-Income Housing Trust Fund, City of Chicago HOME and CDBG entitlement, Neighborhood Opportunity Fund
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: South Side (Englewood, Woodlawn, Bronzeville), West Side (Lawndale, Austin, Humboldt Park), Pilsen, Logan Square-adjacent, Rogers Park, Roseland, Pullman

cities.name: Houston
cities.state_hfa: Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)
cities.jurisdictional_notes: Houston Housing Authority (HHA) administers the local project-based voucher program and is an active affordable housing developer. The City of Houston Housing and Community Development Department administers HOME, CDBG, and local gap financing. TDHCA administers 9% and 4% LIHTC for Texas, with Houston falling in the competitive urban set-aside. Texas does not have a statewide inclusionary zoning mandate, and Houston has no zoning code, making land assembly more flexible but entitlement less predictable than zoned markets.
cities.active_programs_local: Houston Housing Authority project-based vouchers, City of Houston Housing Community Development Department gap financing, HOME and CDBG entitlement, Harvey disaster recovery CDBG-DR funds (winding down), TDHCA 9% and 4% LIHTC allocation
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: Third Ward, Fifth Ward, Second Ward, Acres Homes, Near Northside, Sunnyside, Kashmere Gardens, East End, Near Southeast

cities.name: Dallas
cities.state_hfa: Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)
cities.jurisdictional_notes: Dallas Housing Authority (DHA) is one of the largest PHAs in Texas and actively partners on affordable development. The Dallas Housing Policy 2033 has established affordable housing goals and incentive programs, including a housing trust fund and density bonuses near transit.
cities.active_programs_local: Dallas Housing Authority project-based vouchers, Office of Community Care gap financing, HOME and CDBG entitlement, Dallas Housing Trust Fund, density bonuses near DART transit, TDHCA 9% and 4% LIHTC
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: South Dallas, West Dallas, Pleasant Grove, Hamilton Park, Vickery Meadow, East Dallas, Elm Thicket, Oak Cliff

cities.name: Atlanta
cities.jurisdictional_notes: Atlanta Housing administers the Atlanta Housing Choice Voucher program and project-based vouchers, and is an active partner in mixed-income redevelopment. The City of Atlanta Department of City Planning oversees inclusionary zoning requirements in the Beltline Tax Allocation District. Georgia DCA administers 9% and 4% LIHTC statewide, with Atlanta's metro area receiving the largest share of allocations. Fulton and DeKalb County administer their own HOME entitlement programs, adding local soft debt layers.
cities.active_programs_local: Atlanta Housing project-based vouchers, City of Atlanta Affordable Housing Trust Fund, Beltline Affordable Housing Trust Fund, Invest Atlanta gap financing, HOME and CDBG entitlement (City and County), Georgia DCA LIHTC allocation
cities.typical_submarkets_for_affordable: English Avenue, Vine City, Pittsburgh, Mechanicsville, Summerhill, East Point, Cascade Heights, Southwest Atlanta, Thomasville Heights

cities.name: Miami
cities.jurisdictional_notes: Miami-Dade County Public Housing and Community Development administers local affordable housing programs, HOME, CDBG, and the Surtax program (a dedicated affordable housing levy producing over $30M per year for soft debt).
